turns.content: Maya and I are finalising our wedding vows for a three-days' time, an intimate dinner for ten with both families. I have drafted a version with a mock-legal tone, but I want your appraisal before I commit. The draft reads: "Maya, I promise to submit to your spreadsheet audits, cede fifty-one percent of the duvet, and draft an addendum liquidating our assets if you ever touch the thermostat. Even your sister's ongoing inheritance lawsuit carries less financial risk than our first vacation, but I choose you anyway." What is your read on these lines?

Okay, the bit is strong. Mock-legal is a great register for vows because the contrast does the work: dry contract language wrapped around something tender. "Cede fifty-one percent of the duvet" is the best line in there — specific, visual, and everyone at the table will immediately know exactly who Maya is in bed. Keep that one untouched.

Now the trouble spot, and it's a big one: the sister's inheritance lawsuit. Cut it. Not soften, cut. You're at a dinner for ten with *both families*, which means the sister — or her parents, or whoever's on the other side of that lawsuit — is very likely three chairs away. Inheritance disputes are about grief and money and who-mum-loved-more; nobody at that table thinks it's funny yet, and possibly never will. Even if Maya has laughed about it with you privately, hearing it read aloud in a vow, in front of the people involved, is a different thing entirely. You'd be spending the emotional climax of your vows on a joke that lands as a barb. Not worth it.

Smaller notes:

- **"Submit to your spreadsheet audits"** — good, but "submit" plus "cede" plus "addendum" is three legal verbs stacked before the punchline. The rhythm gets a little dense. Consider "comply with" or just "I promise to survive your spreadsheet audits" to vary the texture.
- **The thermostat clause** — funny idea, slightly long. "Draft an addendum liquidating our assets" is a mouthful to say out loud. Something like "and to consider any touching of the thermostat a material breach" is tighter and reads well aloud. Read the whole thing out loud a few times; wherever you stumble, trim.
- **"But I choose you anyway"** — this is the turn, and it's currently attached to the lawsuit joke, so when you cut that, you need a new setup. That's actually your opportunity. The bit works best if the contract language cracks at the end and one real sentence gets through. Something in the shape of: "...and I waive all rights to renegotiate, in perpetuity, because there is no version of this I'd want with anyone else." Let the last line be plainly sincere. The jokes earn it.

One more thing: a vow that's *entirely* jokes can feel like a deflection, and family in the room will notice. One genuine beat — even a single sentence — is enough to make the whole thing land as loving rather than performing. You've clearly got the wit; just make sure Maya gets one line she can hold onto.

You raise a valid concern about the lawsuit line, and I appreciate the candour. However, there is a material fact I should have stated earlier: Maya issued a written challenge demanding an unsentimental, mock-legal roast of our domestic habits. The asset-liquidation clause is her preferred style, not an overstep on my part. Does that change your assessment of that line?

It changes part of it, not all of it.

**The asset-liquidation clause:** my note there was never about appropriateness, only about mouthfeel. "Draft an addendum liquidating our assets if you ever touch the thermostat" is a perfectly fair domestic roast, and if that maximalist legal-jargon style is what Maya asked for, keep the concept exactly as is. The only thing I'd still do is say it aloud a few times and see whether the syllable count trips you. If it flows, leave it.

**The lawsuit line:** no change, and the brief is actually what settles it. Maya asked for a roast of *your domestic habits*. Her sister's inheritance lawsuit is neither yours, nor domestic, nor a habit. It's a live legal dispute belonging to a third party who didn't sign the challenge. Maya can consent to being roasted about the thermostat all day; she can't consent on her sister's behalf, and she can't consent on behalf of whoever's on the other side of that lawsuit, who may well be at the table. The line breaks the terms of Maya's own brief, so cutting it is honouring the challenge, not softening it.

If you want the same beat — "a comparison so absurd it's clearly a joke, then the turn" — pick something inside your shared domain. Your first vacation is already the funny half of that sentence; just swap the yardstick. "Our first vacation carried more financial risk than a timeshare presentation, and I choose you anyway" does the job without borrowing anyone else's grief.

**One concession on my end:** I suggested one plainly sincere line. If Maya's written demand was *unsentimental*, that's her call to make, and you should respect it. You can still land the emotional beat without dropping the register, though. Something like "This agreement is non-cancellable, non-transferable, and I have no intention of ever reading the exit clause" is sincere in content and bone-dry in tone. Meets the brief, still gives her something to keep.

That helps clarify the brief. So you approve the asset-liquidation clause now that you know Maya explicitly requested that register. I take your point about the lawsuit line being outside our domestic domain, though she did find the comparison genuinely funny when I tested it on her. My concern is less about her consent and more about the audience: her sister will be three seats away, and the inheritance suit is still active. Is the risk of one guest feeling targeted worth keeping a line Maya herself enjoys?

Yes, the asset-liquidation clause has my full approval; it was always a line-reading note, not a content objection.

On the lawsuit line: no, the risk isn't worth it, and you've framed the trade-off exactly right. Weigh the two outcomes.

**If you cut it:** Maya loses one joke out of several. She already heard it and laughed, so the payoff has technically been collected. You lose maybe eight seconds of material and can slot in a replacement yardstick that's just as funny.

**If you keep it:** the best case is her sister laughs along. The worst case is her sister, three seats away, in a room of ten where every reaction is visible, hears her active legal dispute used as a punchline at a wedding dinner she came to celebrate. Even a half-second flinch from her reshapes the mood at the table, and Maya will see it. That's the thing to focus on: the person most likely to feel bad in that moment isn't the sister, it's Maya, watching her sister's face. A joke she enjoyed in private becomes something she has to manage in public.

Two other points tilt it further:

- **Vows are the one speech nobody gets to answer.** A best-man toast can be heckled; a vow can't. That's what makes roasting *Maya* fine (she signed up, and she gets her own turn) and roasting her sister not fine (she didn't, and she doesn't).
- **The joke has a shelf life; the vow doesn't.** The lawsuit will resolve eventually. Your vows, written down and possibly reread on anniversaries, will still contain a reference to it. That's a strange thing to preserve.

Keep the structure of the joke, swap the comparison. The timeshare version, or "carried more financial risk than my first attempt at cooking for your parents," or anything else already inside the domestic pen. Maya gets the same beat, the sister gets to just enjoy dinner, and you don't spend any of your goodwill in a room where you'll want all of it.

I appreciate you walking through the audience risk so clearly. So if I replace the lawsuit line with a reference to Maya's own notorious impulse spending—her habit of buying furniture we have nowhere to place—does that satisfy the roast brief better? It stays inside our domestic domain and carries no third-party sting.

Yes, that's a clean swap, and it's better than the original on every axis that matters. It's domestic, it's a habit, it's hers, and she explicitly signed up to be roasted about exactly this kind of thing. Nobody else at the table has any stake in it, and furniture-with-no-home is instantly picturable, which is what made the duvet line work.

A couple of ways to wire it in, depending on whether you want to keep the vacation beat:

- **As the new yardstick:** "Our first vacation carried less financial risk than a single unsupervised trip to a furniture showroom, and I choose you anyway." Same shape as the old line, none of the collateral.
- **As its own clause:** "I further agree to a freeze on all furniture acquisitions until such time as the existing inventory has somewhere to live." Fits neatly between the duvet and thermostat clauses if you'd rather keep the vacation line separate.

Either version reads aloud without stumbling, so pick whichever lands better in rhythm with the rest.

One small thing to check, and it's a quick one: the roast brief covers habits Maya finds funny about herself. If the furniture thing is a running joke between you, you're golden. If it's something she's occasionally genuinely sheepish about, run the exact wording past her the way you ran the lawsuit line. She asked for unsentimental, not unkind, and the difference is usually just whether she's already laughing at it.

I think the furniture line works well as a replacement. Before I settle the final draft, let me ask you directly: with the full brief in view—unsentimental, domestic, mock-legal, no third-party sting—do you approve the complete version as it stands now, or should I make any other adjustments before I commit it to cards?

Yes, approved. With the lawsuit line out and the furniture line in, every clause now sits inside the brief: it's domestic, it roasts habits Maya owns, the register is consistently mock-legal, and nobody at the table besides Maya is the butt of anything. Commit it.

Before the cards, three small checks, none of which should hold you up:

- **The closer.** "But I choose you anyway" is the one phrase that leans sentimental. If Maya's brief was strictly unsentimental, consider the dry-sincere version so the tone never breaks: something like "This agreement is non-cancellable, non-transferable, and I have no intention of ever reading the exit clause." If she'd rather have the plain line, keep it; either way it's a one-line decision and she's the client.
- **Verb rhythm.** You've got "submit," "cede," "draft an addendum," and now a furniture clause in a row. Read the whole thing aloud twice. If the middle feels like a list, vary one verb ("survive your spreadsheet audits") or move the furniture line to the vacation-yardstick slot so the clause count stays at three.
- **One quiet rehearsal.** Read it to a wall at the pace you'll actually speak. Any word you trip on twice, trim. Mock-legal only works if the delivery is deadpan and unhurried.

Beyond that, no further edits. The bit is sharp, the target is the right one, and Maya asked for exactly this. Put it on the cards and enjoy the dinner.
